title: Challenge 01: Find Your Way Around
description: Repository orientation, headings, tabs, file tree navigation, and confidence in the Learning Room.
concepts: Repository orientation, headings, tabs, file tree navigation, and confidence in the Learning Room.
Challenge title: Find Your Way Around
transcriptText:
[ALEX]
Welcome back. Today we're helping you build a mental map of GitHub, then use that map inside your own Learning Room repository, and finally apply it to the first scavenger-hunt style challenge.

[JAMIE]
I like that order, because GitHub can feel huge at first. If I'm blind or low vision and I land on a page full of links, buttons, tabs, and tables, what do I need to know first so I don't panic?

[ALEX]
The first big idea is that GitHub is not one single page pattern. It has levels. Think of three nested layers. Level one is your own account area, like your profile, notifications, or settings. Level two is an organization or user space, like a company or project owner. Level three is a repository, and that is where most workshop work happens.

[JAMIE]
So when someone says, go to the repo, they mean that third level.

[ALEX]
Exactly. And that matters because repositories contain the things you'll work with directly: code, issues, pull requests, actions, branches, files, and project documentation.

[JAMIE]
What's the fastest way to tell which level I'm on?

[ALEX]
Use three signals every time. First, the URL. Second, the browser tab title. Third, the first level one heading.

[JAMIE]
Let's unpack that.

[ALEX]
If the URL is just github dot com, you're likely on your feed or home area. If it's github dot com slash username, you're on a profile. If it's github dot com slash owner slash repo, you're on a repository home page, usually the Code tab. Add slash issues and you're on the issues list. Add slash issues slash a number and you're on one issue. Add slash pull slash a number and you're on one pull request. If you see tree in the URL, you're in a folder. If you see blob, you're in a file. If you see commit, you're on a commit page.

[JAMIE]
And the browser title follows patterns too, right?

[ALEX]
Yes. Repository home pages usually sound like owner slash repo, then a short description, then GitHub. Issues lists sound like Issues dot owner slash repo. Issue detail pages include the issue title and number. Pull requests do the same. Notifications and settings also have predictable titles.

[JAMIE]
And then the heading trick.

[ALEX]
If you press the key to move to heading level one, what you hear tells you the page type. On a repository page, you hear owner slash repo-name. On an issues list, you hear Issues. On an issue detail page, you hear the issue title. On a pull request detail page, you hear the pull request title. On your profile, your username. On a settings page, the settings category.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Okay, so that already gives me a recovery routine. Check URL, tab title, H1. But what stays the same on every GitHub page?

[ALEX]
The global navigation bar. That top navigation region is your fixed anchor point across GitHub. It usually includes the GitHub home link, search, pull requests, issues, notifications, and your profile menu. The layout may shift depending on screen width, zoom, account state, or feature rollout, but the region is still there.

[JAMIE]
That's an important accessibility point. Don't memorize visual positions too literally.

[ALEX]
Right. Position words like top right or left side are hints, not promises. More reliable anchors are landmark names, tab names, button text, URL patterns, and keyboard shortcuts.

[JAMIE]
What landmark name should screen reader users listen for?

[ALEX]
Navigation Menu. Press your landmark key to cycle until you hear Navigation Menu. Then move by links inside it. The search field is often reachable with slash or S. Notifications can be reached with G then N.

[JAMIE]
And inside a repository there's a second navigation layer.

[ALEX]
Yes. Repository pages add a landmark labeled Repository navigation. That's the row of repo-specific tabs, such as Code, Issues, Pull requests, Actions, Projects, Wiki, Security, Insights, and sometimes Settings if you have permission.

[JAMIE]
So every repo page has the global GitHub layer and then the repository layer.

[ALEX]
That's the core orientation model.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Let's talk page types. If I'm learning GitHub, which page types should I really know cold?

[ALEX]
Five of them. The repository home page, usually the Code tab. The issues list. A single issue detail page. A pull request detail page. And your own feed or profile pages.

[JAMIE]
Start with the repository home page.

[ALEX]
That page is the hub of the project. Expect the repository heading, the repository navigation tabs, branch information, the file tree or files table, a rendered README below the file list if the repo has one, and often an About section with description and metadata.

[JAMIE]
Then the issues list.

[ALEX]
That page has the heading Issues, filters and search tools, and a list of open or closed issues. It's where you scan tasks, bugs, questions, and feature requests.

[JAMIE]
What about an issue detail page?

[ALEX]
That page centers on one issue. You'll hear the issue title as the main heading, then see or hear the issue body, comments, metadata like labels and assignees, and activity over time.

[JAMIE]
And pull request detail pages?

[ALEX]
Very similar, but focused on proposed changes. A pull request detail page often has tabs like Conversation and Files Changed. Conversation shows the description, review comments, checks, and timeline. Files Changed shows the actual diff.

[JAMIE]
Then the personal feed and profile pages are more about your own activity and account space.

[ALEX]
Exactly. Your feed shows activity and updates. Your profile shows your repositories, contributions, and profile information.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Now let's get practical. Suppose I land on a repository page for the first time. What's the orientation sequence?

[ALEX]
Use the same short sequence every time. First, jump to heading level one and confirm the repo name. Second, move through landmarks to learn the main regions. Third, open your heading list or rotor to see the page structure. This gives you a fast map before you begin exploring.

[JAMIE]
What landmark names might show up on a repository page?

[ALEX]
Repository Navigation for the tab bar. Main for the core content like branch selector, file list, repo details, and contributors. And often a region for repository files navigation or rendered README content further down.

[JAMIE]
That's useful because it tells me where the interactive repo controls end and where the actual document content begins.

[ALEX]
Exactly.

[JAMIE]
And heading hierarchy matters too, right?

[ALEX]
Very much. GitHub pages usually have a meaningful heading hierarchy. On repository pages, the H1 is the repo name. Under that, heading level two elements often organize sections like the About area, file list related areas, or README content. On issues and pull requests, the H1 is the item title and lower headings structure comments or side panels. The exact details can change, but headings remain one of the most reliable ways to skim.

[JAMIE]
What about screen size and zoom? Because low-vision learners run into layout shifts all the time.

[ALEX]
GitHub's layout changes by viewport. At full desktop width, controls may appear side by side with a sidebar. At tablet widths, sections may stack or wrap. At mobile widths or very high zoom, tabs can wrap, sidebars can move below the main content, and condensed menus may appear. So again, rely on names, landmarks, and headings more than position.

[JAMIE]
That really is the mental model, isn't it? Not memorize a screenshot. Build an internal map based on stable signals.

[ALEX]
Yes. The goal is to think, I know what kind of page this is, I know the likely landmarks, I know how to confirm where I am, and I know the next region to check.

[JAMIE]
Is there a quick practice drill?

[ALEX]
Yes. Do a sixty-second orientation whenever you land somewhere unfamiliar. Confirm the URL. Listen to the page title. Jump to H1. Cycle landmarks. Open the heading list. Then decide what task you're there to do.

[JAMIE]
And if I get stuck?

[ALEX]
Reset. Go back to URL, H1, and landmarks. If necessary, use browser find, the back button, or a direct shortcut like G then I for Issues or G then P for Pull Requests.

[JAMIE]
I also want to preserve an idea from the reading: learning these manual GitHub features matters later when AI agents enter the picture.

[ALEX]
Absolutely. Issues, labels, pull requests, checks, and workflow automation are also how AI tools operate on GitHub. So when you learn the manual structure, you're also learning the environment your future agents will use.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Let's move from general GitHub structure into repository navigation specifically. What is a repository page in practical terms?

[ALEX]
A repository home page, often called the Code tab, is the project's front door. It brings together the repository heading, the tab bar, branch controls, a file list, optional sidebar information like About, and a rendered README if one exists.

[JAMIE]
And this chapter frames itself as a screen-reader guide, but it still gives guidance for mouse users, low-vision users, and VoiceOver users too.

[ALEX]
Right. One important workshop recommendation here is safety first. This chapter is for confidence building. No grading, no automation check. Learn page structure, practice orientation, confirm readiness with a peer or facilitator, then move into the Learning Room and later issue-based challenges.

[JAMIE]
I appreciate that. It says, build fluency before performance.

[ALEX]
Exactly.

[JAMIE]
So once I'm on a repository page, how do I reach the tabs?

[ALEX]
Find the Repository navigation landmark. Then move through links like Code, Issues, Pull requests, Discussions, Actions, Projects, Wiki, Security, Insights, and Settings if you have maintainer access. Not every repository has every tab enabled.

[JAMIE]
And tab labels often include counts.

[ALEX]
Yes. An Issues tab might announce something like Issues, fourteen open. The current tab is announced as selected or current.

[JAMIE]
Low-vision tip here: at high zoom the tabs may wrap to more than one line, but they remain standard links.

[ALEX]
And keyboard users can still tab through them. Also, GitHub shortcuts like G then I for Issues and G then P for Pull requests can save time.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Now the files table. This is where many learners first feel either empowered or overwhelmed.

[ALEX]
The files table is the heart of the Code tab. It lists folders and files in the current directory. The dependable structure is a table with three main columns: Name, Message, and Age.

[JAMIE]
So the name is the file or folder. Message is the most recent commit message that changed it. Age is how long ago that change happened.

[ALEX]
Correct. For screen reader users, a quick way to reach it is to jump to the next table. Often the first table on the page is the files table. Once in it, use table navigation commands to move row by row and column by column.

[JAMIE]
What's a good way to read one row fully?

[ALEX]
Start in the Name column and hear the file or folder name. Then move right to hear the recent commit message. Move right again for the age. For example, docs slash, Add accessibility guide, three days ago.

[JAMIE]
How do I tell folders from files?

[ALEX]
Folders usually end with a slash in the Name column. Opening a folder reloads the page with that folder's contents. To move back up, use the browser back button or breadcrumb links if present.

[JAMIE]
And for low-vision users, the file list may show icons and truncated text at high zoom, so browser find and Go to file become especially helpful.

[ALEX]
Exactly. The Go to file control, often triggered with T, opens a search interface so you can jump directly to a file name without scanning a long table.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
What about branches?

[ALEX]
The branch selector lets you choose a branch or switch to a tag. On most repository pages there is a branch button near the file list controls. Activate it to open a dropdown. Inside, you can search for branches or tags and choose one.

[JAMIE]
And tags are different from branches.

[ALEX]
Yes. A branch is a moving line of development. A tag is a fixed named snapshot, often used for releases.

[JAMIE]
That distinction matters later when learners start contributing.

[ALEX]
Very much.

[JAMIE]
Now cloning. The source included both GitHub CLI and standard Git.

[ALEX]
Right. Cloning means making a local copy of a repository on your computer. With GitHub CLI, you can clone using the owner slash repo name without typing the full URL. Then change into the folder. With standard Git, you use git clone and the repository URL.

[JAMIE]
So clone is local copy. Not the same as fork.

[ALEX]
Exactly. Fork means create your own copy of someone else's repository under your account or space. Clone means copy a repository to your local machine. Branch means create a separate line of work inside a repository.

[JAMIE]
That trio confuses almost everyone once.

[ALEX]
Yes, but once the distinctions click, many workflows make more sense. Fork if you need your own server-side copy. Clone if you want local files. Branch if you want an isolated stream of changes.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
And then there are repository actions that are not editing actions: watching, starring, and forking.

[ALEX]
Right. Watching subscribes you to notifications. Starring bookmarks the repo as something important to you. Forking creates your own copy for development or experimentation.

[JAMIE]
Let's move to viewing a single file.

[ALEX]
When you open a file from the files table, the file page has its own structure. You'll often find file content, file metadata, and action buttons such as edit, raw view, history, or blame depending on permissions and file type.

[JAMIE]
Markdown files and code files read differently.

[ALEX]
Yes. Markdown files like README dot md often render as formatted content, which is easier to read like a document. Code files usually display line by line in a code view.

[JAMIE]
And there are file action buttons near the file content.

[ALEX]
Yes. Reach them by navigating through links and buttons around the file header area. Editing a file opens GitHub's web editor if you have permission.

[JAMIE]
Then blame view and commit history help answer, who changed this and when?

[ALEX]
Exactly. Blame shows line-by-line authorship, useful for understanding recent changes or finding who touched a line last. Commit history shows a list of commits affecting the repo or file, and an individual commit page shows what changed in that commit.

[JAMIE]
And if I don't want to browse folders manually, I can search for a file.

[ALEX]
Use Go to file. It's one of the fastest ways to navigate a repository, especially with a keyboard or screen reader.

[JAMIE]
There was also mention of a shortcuts spotlight and repository sidebar navigation.

[ALEX]
Yes. GitHub supports repository navigation shortcuts and sometimes a command palette or spotlight style navigation. These tools can reduce hunting and help you jump directly where you need to go.

[JAMIE]
And the About section?

[ALEX]
That area summarizes the repository with description and related metadata. It's useful when you're trying to understand what the project is before digging through files.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Let's make those navigation skills concrete with scenarios.

[ALEX]
Great. If you want to find out what a project does, start at the repository home page, listen to the description, then read the README. If you want a good file to edit, scan docs, contribution guidance, or issues labeled for newcomers. If you want to know who has been working on a file recently, open the file, check blame or history. If you want to understand what changed in the last release, look for tags, releases, and commit history. If you want to contribute, start with the README, contribution docs, issues, and branch workflow.

[JAMIE]
And there's a practical exercise called the five-tab tour.

[ALEX]
Yes. Visit a repository and intentionally explore several tabs, not just Code. That helps learners build a fuller repository map.

[JAMIE]
If they get stuck?

[ALEX]
Go back to the orientation sequence: H1, landmarks, headings, tabs.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Now let's talk about the Learning Room. This is a big administrative and workflow section, and we should not skip any of it.

[ALEX]
Agreed. The Learning Room is your personal practice repository for the workshop. When you accept the GitHub Classroom assignment, GitHub copies a template repository into the workshop organization and creates a private repository just for you, named something like learning-room-your-username.

[JAMIE]
So students are not editing the shared template.

[ALEX]
Correct. You do not work directly in the template repository. The template is the clean master copy maintained by facilitators. Your work happens in your private copy.

[JAMIE]
And every student gets a separate repo.

[ALEX]
Yes, for three reasons: safety, authenticity, and pace. Safety means you can experiment and recover without harming anyone else's work. Authenticity means you practice the real workflow: issues, branches, pull requests, checks, reviews, and merging. Pace means you can move as fast or as slowly as you need.

[JAMIE]
That's a smart design. It makes mistakes normal and private.

[ALEX]
Exactly. Real open source work comes later in a shared space, but the Learning Room helps you build the muscle memory first.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Walk us through the setup steps.

[ALEX]
First, open the GitHub Classroom assignment link provided by the facilitator. You should already be signed into GitHub in the same browser. The link is on classroom dot github dot com. If asked, authorize GitHub Classroom.

[JAMIE]
Then some learners may be asked to identify themselves from a roster.

[ALEX]
Right. If a roster page appears, find your name, select it, and continue. If your name is missing, use the option to skip and then tell the facilitator so they can reconcile it later.

[JAMIE]
Then accept the assignment.

[ALEX]
Activate the Accept this assignment button. GitHub Classroom then creates your private repo from the template and grants you access. This usually takes ten to thirty seconds. Refresh periodically until the repository link appears.

[JAMIE]
Important screen reader tip here: the page may not auto-announce when the repo is ready.

[ALEX]
Exactly. Refresh and scan links until you hear the repository link.

[JAMIE]
Once the repo opens, what should learners verify?

[ALEX]
Three things. The heading matches learning-room-your-username. The About area or description confirms it is your private workshop copy. And you can see expected files and folders such as docs, dot github, and README dot md. Then bookmark the page.

[JAMIE]
Then comes the first challenge issue.

[ALEX]
Yes. Open the Issues tab, using G then I if you like. You should see an open issue titled something like Challenge 1: Find Your Way Around, usually created by an automation bot. Open it and read the instructions.

[JAMIE]
And if Challenge 1 doesn't appear after a couple minutes?

[ALEX]
Refresh once. If it still isn't there, open the Actions tab and check whether the Student Progression Bot workflow ran successfully. If it failed or never ran, send your repo link to the facilitator so they can trigger the workflow or create the issue from the template.

[JAMIE]
Then there's Gandalf.

[ALEX]
Yes. Gandalf is the PR validation bot. Before you even open your first pull request, you can confirm the workflow exists by visiting the Actions tab and looking for a workflow named pr-validation-bot or Gandalf PR Validation. You don't need to run it. You just need to know it's wired up.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
There was also a readiness checkpoint before moving on.

[ALEX]
Right. Before starting later challenge chapters, you should be able to find docs slash CHALLENGES dot md, explain the flow issue to branch to pull request to review to merge, and identify that Gandalf feedback appears on the pull request Conversation tab.

[JAMIE]
The chapter also describes two tracks that reinforce each other.

[ALEX]
Yes. Track one is optional GitHub Skills modules in your own account, such as Introduction to GitHub, Communicate Using Markdown, and Review Pull Requests. Those are self-paced and guided by GitHub's learning bot. Track two is your required Learning Room repository work inside the workshop organization, where the workshop challenges happen.

[JAMIE]
So one is optional skill drills. The other is the required workshop path.

[ALEX]
Exactly. Same GitHub account, different learning environments.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Let's cover the Learning Room structure itself.

[ALEX]
Inside your Learning Room, you'll work with a set of practice files and folders. The docs folder is especially important. It contains files like welcome dot md, keyboard-shortcuts dot md, setup-guide dot md, and CHALLENGES dot md. There may also be bonus challenges.

[JAMIE]
And there is a practice branch concept.

[ALEX]
Yes. You create and use a separate branch for your practice changes. Why? Because branches let you work safely without changing the main branch directly. They support pull requests, review, and clean merges. In other words, the branch is your workbench.

[JAMIE]
How should learners use it?

[ALEX]
Switch to your practice branch before making challenge edits, keep your work there, and use it to open pull requests back into the main branch of your Learning Room repository.

[JAMIE]
Then the practice files are not random. They are designed for specific learning tasks.

[ALEX]
Exactly. For example, docs slash welcome dot md introduces open source contribution and includes TODO items intentionally left for learners in later challenges, such as who can contribute, how to find something to work on, and what happens after your contribution is merged. Keyboard-shortcuts dot md acts as a screen reader shortcut reference. Setup-guide dot md helps learners prepare to contribute. CHALLENGES dot md serves as a challenge menu.

[JAMIE]
That's helpful because students may notice unfinished sections and wonder if something is broken.

[ALEX]
Right. In many cases, those TODOs are intentional and belong to later work.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Now explain how pull request sharing works in the Learning Room, because this is a social and visibility model as much as a technical one.

[ALEX]
A typical flow goes like this. First, the student opens a pull request from their practice branch. Second, an automation bot validates the PR using a workflow, in this case a learning-room PR bot workflow. Third, peer review may be arranged by facilitators. Fourth, the reviewer reads and comments. Fifth, the author responds and updates the PR. Sixth, once the review is approved or the author decides to self-merge according to workshop guidance, the PR is merged and a progression bot posts the next challenge.

[JAMIE]
And visibility matters here.

[ALEX]
Yes. Learners need to know what they can and cannot see. Your Learning Room repository is private to you unless access is intentionally shared for peer review or buddy work. In normal use, other students do not automatically see your repo, and you do not automatically see theirs.

[JAMIE]
So peer simulation issues inside your own repo provide realistic practice even without broad visibility.

[ALEX]
Exactly. And when a real peer reviewer is paired with you, visibility is intentionally arranged.

[JAMIE]
The chapter also separates kinds of feedback by timing.

[ALEX]
Right. Type one is automated bot feedback, often arriving within about thirty seconds. Type two is peer reviewer feedback, which may take fifteen to sixty minutes. Type three is progress tracking after merge, where the system unlocks or posts the next challenge.

[JAMIE]
There are also optional study groups.

[ALEX]
Yes. Those are optional and can support discussion and mutual help, but the core workflow still lives in each learner's own repository.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
What key differences should learners remember between a GitHub Skills module and the Learning Room?

[ALEX]
Skills modules are optional, self-paced exercises under your account with GitHub's learning bot. The Learning Room is the required workshop track, inside the workshop organization, using your private classroom repository, the workshop challenge sequence, and workshop automation like Gandalf and progression bots.

[JAMIE]
Then there are tips for reviewing a peer's PR.

[ALEX]
Yes. Find the PR you've been assigned or invited to review. Read the Conversation tab for context. Read the changed files. Leave a review with comments that are specific, kind, and actionable. If you are the author receiving feedback, respond clearly and update your branch.

[JAMIE]
That matters for accessible collaboration too. Reviews should help, not gatekeep.

[ALEX]
Absolutely.

[JAMIE]
Let's do the FAQ lightning round.

[ALEX]
Sure. Can you see other students' PRs? Not by default, only when access is intentionally arranged. What if you disagree with your assigned reviewer? Discuss respectfully and ask a facilitator if needed. Will your PR get lost when everyone is working at once? The workflow is designed to track progress, so no, it should not simply disappear. Can you comment on someone else's PR? Only if you have access and the facilitator has arranged that interaction. What if your reviewer doesn't respond? Follow workshop guidance and contact a facilitator. Can you work with a friend? Sometimes, if that is intentionally allowed. How long does review take? It varies, with bot feedback arriving quickly and human review taking longer. What if bot feedback is wrong? Treat the bot as helpful automation, not infallible truth, and ask a facilitator when something seems off. Do you need to complete every challenge? Follow workshop expectations, but the structure is designed as a guided progression.

[JAMIE]
And if learners get stuck in the Learning Room?

[ALEX]
Use the repo map, ask a facilitator, check Issues and Actions, and remember that the point is learning, not silent struggle.

[JAMIE]
I love the spirit of the closing idea here: you're contributing.

[ALEX]
Yes. Even inside a practice repo, you're learning the real habits of contribution.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Now let's connect all that to the first challenge itself.

[ALEX]
Challenge 1 is called Find Your Way Around. It is a scavenger hunt in your Learning Room repository. The goal is not to memorize exact counts or pass a trick question. The goal is to become familiar with repository navigation.

[JAMIE]
What are learners asked to do?

[ALEX]
They explore the Learning Room repository and gather evidence. Specifically, find the Code tab and count how many items are in the root of the repository, open the Issues tab and find an open issue, navigate to docs slash welcome dot md and read the first paragraph, find the repository description near the top of the Code tab, locate README dot md and identify who the workshop is for, and find the About information area associated with the repository.

[JAMIE]
Then they paste short evidence statements into the issue.

[ALEX]
Exactly. The evidence can be simple. For example: I found a certain number of root items. The open issue I found was titled blank. The first paragraph of welcome dot md says blank. The repository description is blank. The README says the workshop is for blank. The About section shows blank.

[JAMIE]
There's also a peer simulation step.

[ALEX]
Yes. After submitting evidence, learners should open the peer simulation issue called Welcome Link Needs Context and leave an encouraging comment or reaction. If a facilitator has provided a real buddy repository, they may use that issue instead.

[JAMIE]
That's a nice early nudge toward community behavior, not just navigation.

[ALEX]
Exactly. Technical orientation and social participation go together.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
What if someone gets stuck during the scavenger hunt?

[ALEX]
There are concrete suggestions. If you cannot find the tabs, look for the horizontal repository navigation below the repository name, or for screen reader users, navigate by heading level two or landmarks. If you cannot find docs slash welcome dot md, start on the Code tab, open the docs folder, then open welcome dot md. If you are not sure what counts as evidence, any reasonable description of what you found is acceptable. And if you want to check your work, there is a reference solution.

[JAMIE]
Let's go through that solution carefully, because it teaches what matters.

[ALEX]
On the Code tab, expected findings include common root items like README dot md, the docs folder, and the dot github folder. The exact count may vary as the repository evolves, so any reasonable count is acceptable.

[JAMIE]
That's important. This is not a gotcha over one number.

[ALEX]
Right. On the Issues tab, you should find at least one open issue. If no issues are open at that moment, simply noting that the tab exists can still demonstrate orientation.

[JAMIE]
And docs slash welcome dot md?

[ALEX]
Its first paragraph introduces the Learning Room and what students will do. Learners may also notice TODO comments, and those are intentional for a later challenge.

[JAMIE]
Then the description and README.

[ALEX]
The repository description appears near the top of the Code tab below the repository name. The README renders automatically below the file list. That README tells learners who the workshop is for.

[JAMIE]
The solution also mentions alternate approaches.

[ALEX]
Yes. You can browse on github dot com through the tabbed interface. You can press period on a repository page to open github dot dev and use the Explorer sidebar. You can use VS Code with the GitHub Repositories extension to browse remotely. Or use GitHub CLI, for example gh repo view owner slash repo dash dash web, to open the repository in the browser.

[JAMIE]
And the takeaway?

[ALEX]
What matters is familiarity with repository navigation, not memorizing an exact file count. If you explored the tabs and found the key files, you completed the learning goal.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Before we close, I want to preserve the administrative source notes too.

[ALEX]
Good catch. Across these readings, learners are repeatedly pointed to authoritative sources when GitHub's interface changes: GitHub Docs, the GitHub Changelog, GitHub's accessibility documentation, the repository accessibility guide, and official documentation about repositories, README files, editing files, Git, GitHub Flow, and pull requests. The reason is simple: GitHub evolves. Your mental model should be stable, but if a button moves or a workflow label changes, the official docs are the source of truth.

[JAMIE]
So the durable lesson is structure, not screenshot memorization.

[ALEX]
Exactly. Build an internal map using URL, title, H1, landmarks, tabs, tables, branch controls, file views, issues, and pull requests. Then practice that map in your private Learning Room. Then use Challenge 1 to prove to yourself that you can find your way around.

[JAMIE]
And if you can do that, you've already crossed one of the biggest early barriers: GitHub no longer feels like a maze.

[ALEX]
Beautifully said.

[PAUSE]

[ALEX]
For your next step, open your Learning Room repository, orient yourself using H1 and landmarks, visit Code and Issues, open docs slash welcome dot md, read the README, and complete your scavenger hunt evidence. Then leave that encouraging peer simulation comment.

[JAMIE]
You do not need perfect recall. You need a repeatable way to get oriented.

[ALEX]
And now you have one.

        ## Challenge 1: Find Your Way Around

        **Chapters:** [Ch02: Understanding GitHub](https://github.com/Community-Access/git-going-with-github/blob/main/docs/02-understanding-github.md) | [Ch03: Navigating Repositories](https://github.com/Community-Access/git-going-with-github/blob/main/docs/03-navigating-repositories.md) | [Ch04: The Learning Room](https://github.com/Community-Access/git-going-with-github/blob/main/docs/04-the-learning-room.md)

        **What you will do:** Explore this learning-room repository like a scavenger hunt. You will navigate tabs, the file tree, read key files, and find landmarks.

        ### Step-by-step scavenger hunt

        **Task 1: Count files in the root**
        1. Make sure you are on the **Code** tab (click it at the top)
        2. Look at the file/folder list
        3. Count how many items are showing (stop before the first folder)
        4. Write down this number

        **Task 2: Find an open issue**
        1. Click the **Issues** tab
        2. Look for issues with a green **Open** label
        3. Click on one to read it
        4. Write down its title

        **Task 3: Read welcome.md**
        1. Click the **Code** tab
        2. Look for a folder named `docs/`
        3. Click to open it
        4. Find `welcome.md` and click it
        5. Read the first paragraph (the opening sentence)
        6. Write down what it says

        **Task 4: Find the repo description**
        1. Go to the **Code** tab
        2. Look at the top-right area - you should see a text description under the repo name
        3. This is the "About" section
        4. Write down what it says

        **Task 5: Read the README**
        1. On the **Code** tab, scroll down to find `README.md`
        2. Click it to open
        3. Find the section that says "Who this workshop is for"
        4. Write down the answer

        **Task 6: Check the About section**
        1. On the **Code** tab, look at the right sidebar
        2. You should see a section labeled "About" with repo information
        3. Write down what you see there

  - type: textarea
    id: evidence
    attributes:
      label: "Your evidence"
      description: "Paste your scavenger hunt findings below. For each item, write a short sentence about what you found."
      placeholder: |
        1. I found ___ files in the root of the repository.
        2. The open issue I found was titled "___".
        3. The first paragraph of welcome.md says...
        4. The repository description is...
        5. The README says this workshop is for...
        6. The About section shows...
    validations:
      required: true

  - type: markdown
    attributes:
      value: |
        ### Peer simulation check

        After you submit your evidence, open the **Peer Simulation: Welcome Link Needs Context** issue in this repository and leave an encouraging comment or reaction. If your facilitator gave you access to a real buddy repository, you may use your buddy's issue instead.

        ### If you get stuck

        | Symptom | Try this |
        |---|---|
        | I cannot find the tabs | Look for a horizontal navigation bar below the repository name. Screen reader users: navigate by heading level 2 or use the landmark navigation. |
        | I cannot find `docs/welcome.md` | On the Code tab, look for a folder called `docs`. Select it, then select `welcome.md`. |
        | I am not sure what counts as evidence | Any description of what you found works. There are no wrong answers in a scavenger hunt. |
        | I finished but want to check my work | [View the reference solution](https://github.com/Community-Access/git-going-with-github/blob/main/docs/solutions/solution-01-scavenger-hunt.md) |

# Solution Reference: Challenge 1 -- Find Your Way Around

This is one way the scavenger hunt could look. Your exact findings will vary depending on when you completed the challenge. If you found the key elements, you succeeded.

## Expected findings

### Code tab

- The root of the repository contains files like `README.md`, `docs/`, and `.github/`
- The file count varies as the repository evolves -- any reasonable count is correct

### Issues tab

- You should have found at least one open issue
- If no issues were open, noting that the tab exists is sufficient

### docs/welcome.md

- The first paragraph introduces the learning room and what students will do
- You may have noticed TODO comments -- those are intentionally left for Challenge 2

### Repository description and README

- The description appears at the top of the Code tab, below the repository name
- The README renders automatically below the file list

## Alternate approaches

- **github.com:** Click each tab in the top navigation bar
- **github.dev:** Press `.` on any repo page to open the web editor, then use the Explorer sidebar
- **VS Code with GitHub extension:** Use the GitHub Repositories extension to browse remotely
- **GitHub CLI:** `gh repo view Community-Access/git-going-with-github --web` opens the repo in a browser

## What matters

The learning objective is familiarity with repository navigation, not memorizing exact file counts. If you explored the tabs and found the key files, you completed this challenge.

## Authoritative Sources

Use these official references when you need the current source of truth for facts in this chapter.

- [GitHub Docs, home](https://docs.github.com/en)
- [GitHub Changelog](https://github.blog/changelog/)

# Understanding GitHub's Web Structure
>
> **Listen to Episode 2:** [Understanding GitHub on the Web](https://lp.csedesigns.com/ggg/PODCASTS.html) - a conversational audio overview of this chapter. Listen before reading to preview the concepts, or after to reinforce what you learned.

> **Related appendices:** [Appendix A: Glossary](appendix-a-glossary.md) | [Appendix B: Screen Reader Cheat Sheet](appendix-b-screen-reader-cheatsheet.md)
> **Authoritative sources:** [GitHub Docs: About GitHub](https://docs.github.com/en/get-started/start-your-journey/about-github-and-git) | [GitHub Accessibility Documentation](https://accessibility.github.com/documentation)

## How GitHub Is Organized, and How to Orient Yourself on Every Page

> **Read this before navigating GitHub for the first time.** This lesson gives you the mental model that makes every subsequent guide easier. Once you understand how GitHub pages are built - their landmark structure, heading hierarchy, and URL patterns - you will know how to orient yourself on any page you land on, even ones this guide never mentions.

## Table of Contents

> **Challenge 1: Find Your Way Around** uses the concepts from this chapter and [Chapter 03](03-navigating-repositories.md) and [Chapter 04](04-the-learning-room.md). Read this chapter first to build the mental model, then navigate repositories with confidence.

1. [GitHub's Three-Level Structure](#1-githubs-three-level-structure)
2. [What Is Always on Every GitHub Page](#2-what-is-always-on-every-github-page)
3. [How to Tell Where You Are](#3-how-to-tell-where-you-are)
4. [The Five Key Page Types](#4-the-five-key-page-types)
5. [Visual Map of a Repository Page](#5-visual-map-of-a-repository-page)
6. [Screen Reader Orientation Sequence](#6-screen-reader-orientation-sequence)
7. [Landmark Structure by Page Type](#7-landmark-structure-by-page-type)
8. [GitHub's Heading Hierarchy in Practice](#8-githubs-heading-hierarchy-in-practice)
9. [How GitHub's Layout Changes by Viewport](#9-how-githubs-layout-changes-by-viewport)
10. [The Mental Model - Building Your Internal Map](#10-the-mental-model---building-your-internal-map)

> **The Capstone Connection:** By the end of tomorrow, you will build your own customized AI Agent. But agents do not have magic portals into your code — they read Issues, they write Pull Requests, and they trigger on Labels. Think of GitHub as the operating system for AI. As you learn these manual features today, you are actually learning how to converse with the agents you will build tomorrow.

## 1. GitHub's Three-Level Structure

GitHub is not a single page or a single kind of page. It is three nested levels, and understanding which level you are on changes how you navigate.

```text
    Level 1: Your Account / Profile
   github.com/your-username
   github.com/settings/...
   github.com/notifications

Level 2: An Organization or User's Space
   github.com/microsoft
   github.com/community-access
   github.com/github

Level 3: A Repository - where all the work happens
   github.com/community-access/accessibility-agents
   github.com/community-access/accessibility-agents/issues
   github.com/community-access/accessibility-agents/pull/42
```

**Most of this workshop happens at Level 3.** Issues, pull requests, code, and actions all live inside a repository. When someone says "go to the repo," they mean Level 3.

> **Screen reader orientation tip:** The first heading (`H` then `1`) on any page tells you what level you are on. On a repository page, it reads "owner/repo-name." On your profile page, it reads your username. On a settings page, it reads the settings category name.

## 2. What Is Always on Every GitHub Page

No matter where you navigate on GitHub, the same global navigation bar is at the top of every page. Understanding its landmark structure means you always have a fixed orientation point.

> **Dependable walkthrough principle:** GitHub changes visual placement, density, wrapping, and feature rollout over time. Treat position words such as "top-right," "left side," "first," and "below" as orientation hints only. For reliable teaching, anchor each step on the stable thing a learner can verify: URL pattern, page title, H1 heading, landmark name, tab name, keyboard shortcut, command name, or button text.

### The Global Navigation Bar (always present)

Visually, the top bar commonly contains the following controls. The order and compactness can change with viewport width, account state, and product rollout:

| Element | What It Is | How to Reach It |
| ---  | ---  | ---  |
| GitHub logo / home link | Returns to your personal feed | First link in "Navigation Menu" landmark |
| Search bar | Global search across all of GitHub | `S` or `/` shortcut; or `D` → Navigation Menu → `K` to search |
| Copilot icon | Quick access to GitHub Copilot chat | `K` navigation from search bar |
| Pull Requests | Your PRs across all repos | `K` navigation |
| Issues | Your issues across all repos | `K` navigation |
| Notifications (bell) | Your notification inbox | `G` then `N` shortcut |
| Profile avatar | Account menu, settings, sign out | `K` to last link in nav; or go directly via URL |

**Screen reader landmark:** All of these live inside the landmark labeled **"Navigation Menu"**. Press `D` to cycle landmarks until you hear "Navigation Menu," then press `K` to move through the links inside it.

> **Important:** These are standard anchor links. You do not need to switch to Focus Mode to activate them. Press `Enter` in Browse Mode and they work.

### Secondary navigation (repository pages only)

When you are inside a repository, a second navigation bar appears below the global bar. This contains the repository's tabs: Code, Issues, Pull requests, Actions, Projects, Wiki, Security, Insights, and Settings.

**Screen reader landmark:** This is labeled **"Repository navigation"**. Press `D` to jump to it directly.

### Learning Cards: What Is Always on Every GitHub Page

<details>
<summary>Screen reader users</summary>

- Press `D` to cycle landmarks; the first landmark on every page is "Navigation Menu" -- this is your fixed anchor point
- Press `G` then `N` (two keystrokes in sequence) to jump directly to Notifications from any GitHub page
- The global search field is reachable with `S` or `/`; after searching, results load into the Main landmark -- press `D` to jump there

</details>

<details>
<summary>Low vision users</summary>

- The global navigation bar is pinned to the top of every page; at 200%+ zoom it may shrink icons but keeps all items in a single row
- The notification bell shows an unread count as a blue dot (or a number badge); zoom in on the top-right corner to see it clearly
- Repository tabs below the global bar highlight the active tab with a colored underline; switch to a high-contrast theme if the underline is hard to see

</details>

<details>
<summary>Sighted users</summary>

- The global nav bar runs across the top: GitHub logo (left), search bar (center), and profile avatar/bell icon (right)
- Inside a repository, a second row of tabs (Code, Issues, Pull requests, etc.) appears below the global bar; the active tab has a bold underline
- The notification bell icon in the top-right shows a blue dot when you have unread notifications

</details>

## 3. How to Tell Where You Are

Three signals tell you exactly where you are on GitHub, without needing to see the visual layout:

### Signal 1: The URL

GitHub URLs are readable descriptions of your location:

| URL pattern | Where you are |
| ---  | ---  |
| `github.com` | Your personal feed / home |
| `github.com/username` | A user profile page |
| `github.com/org` | An organization profile |
| `github.com/owner/repo` | Repository home page (Code tab) |
| `github.com/owner/repo/issues` | Issues list |
| `github.com/owner/repo/issues/42` | A specific issue (number 42) |
| `github.com/owner/repo/pull/7` | A specific pull request (number 7) |
| `github.com/owner/repo/tree/main/docs` | A folder inside the repo |
| `github.com/owner/repo/blob/main/README.md` | A specific file |
| `github.com/owner/repo/commit/a1b2c3d` | A specific commit |
| `github.com/settings/accessibility` | Your accessibility settings |
| `github.com/notifications` | Your notification inbox |

**Screen reader tip:** Your browser's address bar is always reachable with `Alt+D` (Windows) or `Cmd+L` (Mac). Press it, listen to the URL, and you will know exactly where you are.

### Signal 2: The browser tab title

GitHub formats page titles consistently:

| Page type | Title format |
| ---  | ---  |
| Repository home | `owner/repo: Short description - GitHub` |
| Issues list | `Issues · owner/repo` |
| Specific issue | `Issue title · Issue #42 · owner/repo` |
| Pull request | `PR title · Pull Request #7 · owner/repo` |
| Your notifications | `Notifications - GitHub` |
| Settings | `Category - Settings` |

### Signal 3: The first H1 heading

Press `1` (in Browse Mode) on any GitHub page to jump to the first H1 heading. What you hear tells you what type of page you are on:

| You hear | You are on |
| ---  | ---  |
| `owner/repo-name` | Repository home page |
| `Issues` | Issues list |
| The issue title | Issue detail page |
| The PR title | Pull request detail page |
| Your username | Your profile page |
| A settings category name | A settings page |

## 4. The Five Key Page Types

### Page Type 1: Repository Home (Code Tab)

This is the central hub of any project. It is where you find the file tree, the README, branch information, and links to all other parts of the repository.

#### What to expect

- H1: `owner/repo-name`
- Repository navigation landmark (Code, Issues, PRs, Actions tabs)
- A file tree table - navigate with `T` then `Ctrl+Alt+Arrow`
- A rendered README below the file tree
- A sidebar with About, Topics, Releases, Contributors

### Page Type 2: Issues List

A searchable, filterable list of all issues in the repository.

#### What to expect

- H1: `Issues`
- A search and filter bar at the top
- Each issue is a link with: issue title, labels, number, author, comment count
- Issue titles are H3 headings - press `3` to jump between them
- Landmark: "Search Results List"

### Page Type 3: Issue Detail

The full view of a single issue: the original report, all comments, labels, assignees, and the timeline.

#### What to expect

- H1: The issue title
- H2: "Description" (original issue body)
- H2: "Activity" (comments and events)
- Landmark: "Add a comment" (the reply box at the bottom)
- Sidebar: assignees, labels, milestone, linked PRs

### Page Type 4: Pull Request Detail

The most complex page on GitHub - it has three tabs (Conversation, Commits, Files Changed), each with its own structure.

#### What to expect

- H1: The PR title
- Landmark: "Pull request tabs" (Conversation, Commits, Files changed)
- Conversation tab: same structure as an issue detail
- Files Changed tab: a file tree on the left + diff view on the right
- Landmark: "Pull request navigation tabs" - use `D` to reach it, then `Left`/`Right Arrow` to switch tabs

### Page Type 5: Your Personal Feed and Profile

Your personal home (`github.com`) shows activity from repositories you follow. Your profile (`github.com/username`) shows your contribution graph, pinned repos, and bio.

#### What to expect on your feed

- A "For you" activity stream - recent activity from repos you watch
- A sidebar of suggested repositories and topics

#### What to expect on your profile

- H1: Your username
- A contribution activity graph (visually prominent; read as a table by screen readers)
- Pinned repositories
- A list of your recent public activity

### Learning Cards: The Five Key Page Types

<details>
<summary>Screen reader users</summary>

- On the Repository Home page, press `T` to jump to the file table, then `Ctrl+Alt+Down Arrow` to walk through files row by row
- On an Issue Detail page, press `3` to jump between H3 comment headers; each announces the author and timestamp
- On the PR Files Changed tab, press `3` to jump between file name headings; press `4` to jump between diff hunk headers inside each file

</details>

<details>
<summary>Low vision users</summary>

- On the Repository Home page, the file tree uses alternating row shading; enable a high-contrast theme if rows blend together
- Issue labels appear as small colored badges next to each title in the Issues list; zoom to 150%+ so the label text is readable
- On the PR Files Changed tab, additions are shaded green and deletions are shaded red; high-contrast themes use bolder shading

</details>

<details>
<summary>Sighted users</summary>

- The Repository Home page has a two-column layout: file tree on the left, About sidebar on the right, and README rendered below both
- The Issues list shows a green "Open" or red "Closed" icon next to each issue title, plus label badges and comment count icons
- Pull request tabs (Conversation, Commits, Files changed) appear as a horizontal bar just below the PR title

</details>

## 5. Visual Map of a Repository Page

> **See also:** [Appendix A: Glossary](appendix-a-glossary.md) defines every term used in this course. [Appendix B: Screen Reader Cheat Sheet](appendix-b-screen-reader-cheatsheet.md) has quick-reference keyboard shortcuts for navigating headings and landmarks.

### Description

A repository home page is laid out from top to bottom as follows. The Global Navigation bar (landmark: "Navigation Menu") contains the GitHub logo, Search, Copilot, Pull Requests, Issues, Notifications bell, and your avatar. Below that are the Repository Tabs (landmark: "Repository navigation") showing Code, Issues (12), Pull requests (3), Actions, and more. Next is the Repository Header, which is the H1 heading "owner / repo-name" plus Star (42), Watch, and Fork (8) buttons. The main content area is split into two columns. On the left is the File Area with the branch selector (main), Go to file button, Code button, and the File Table (a landmark) listing files like .github/, docs/, and README.md with dates. On the right is the Sidebar with the About section, description text, topics (accessibility), Releases (3), Contributors (5), and Languages (Markdown 100%). Below both columns is the rendered README (landmark: "Repository files navigation"), and at the bottom is the Footer.

### Screen reader navigation of this page

Press 1 to hear "owner/repo-name" (the H1, confirms you are on the right repo). Press D to hear "Navigation Menu," then D again for "Repository navigation," then D again for "Main" (the file tree area). Press T to jump to the file table, then Ctrl+Alt+Down Arrow to navigate rows. Press D again to reach "Repository files navigation" and read the README.

## 6. Screen Reader Orientation Sequence

Do this every time you land on a new GitHub page. It takes about 10 seconds once you are practiced. Make it automatic.

<details>
<summary>Visual / mouse users - page orientation</summary>

When you land on a GitHub page, scan these areas to orient yourself:

1. **Browser tab title** - tells you the page type and repo context
2. **Global nav bar** (top strip) - GitHub logo, search box, bells/icons
3. **Repo tabs** (below global nav, visible only inside a repo) - Code, Issues, Pull Requests, etc.
4. **H1 heading** - tells you exactly what page you're on (repo name / "Issues" / issue title / PR title)
5. **Main content area** - file tree, issue list, PR diff, etc.

That's your visual map. Click anything visible to navigate.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Screen reader users (NVDA / JAWS) - 10-second orientation sequence</summary>

```text
Step 1: Press 1
        → Hear: what page type are you on? (repo name / "Issues" / issue title / PR title)

Step 2: Press D repeatedly
        → Hear: what landmark regions exist on this page?
        → Build a map: "Navigation Menu, Repository navigation, Main, Add a comment, Pagination"

Step 3: Press NVDA+F7 (NVDA) or Insert+F3 (JAWS)
        → Open the Elements List → choose "Headings" tab
        → Hear: the full heading outline of the page
        → This tells you every major section available
```

After these three steps, you know:

- **What** page you are on (step 1)
- **Where** the page regions are (step 2)
- **What** content is available and how it is organized (step 3)

From there, navigate with purpose: `D` to jump to regions, `H` or `3` to jump to content headings, `K` for links, `B` for buttons.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Screen reader users (VoiceOver - macOS) - 10-second orientation sequence</summary>

```text
Step 1: Quick Nav H (with Quick Nav on) or VO+Cmd+H → navigate to h1
        → Hear: what page type are you on? (repo name / "Issues" / issue title / PR title)

Step 2: VO+U → press Left/Right Arrow to choose "Landmarks" → Up/Down to explore
        → Build a map: "Navigation Menu, Repository navigation, Main, Add a comment, Pagination"
        → Escape to dismiss the rotor

Step 3: VO+U → press Left/Right Arrow to choose "Headings"
        → Hear: the full heading outline of the page
        → Up/Down to navigate headings; Enter to jump to one
```

After these three steps, you know:

- **What** page you are on (step 1)
- **Where** the page regions are (step 2)
- **What** content is available and how it is organized (step 3)

From there, navigate with purpose: `VO+U → Landmarks` to jump to regions, Quick Nav `H` to jump to content headings, Quick Nav `K` for links, Quick Nav `B` for buttons.

> **VoiceOver tip:** `VO` = `Control+Option`. Turn Quick Nav on/off by pressing `Left Arrow + Right Arrow` simultaneously. Quick Nav lets you use single keys (`H`, `B`, `K`, `T`) without holding `VO`, matching the feel of NVDA/JAWS browse mode.

</details>

### Learning Cards: Screen Reader Orientation Sequence

<details>
<summary>Screen reader users</summary>

- Make the three-step sequence automatic: `1` (hear H1), `D D D` (hear landmarks), `NVDA+F7` or `Insert+F3` (see headings list)
- VoiceOver users: `VO+U` then arrow to "Landmarks" replaces the `D` key; `VO+U` then arrow to "Headings" replaces `NVDA+F7`
- If pressing `1` reads something unexpected, you may be inside a modal or dialog; press `Escape` first, then try `1` again

</details>

<details>
<summary>Low vision users</summary>

- Use the browser tab title as a quick orientation check without scrolling; it always shows the page type and repository context
- Press `Alt+D` (Windows) or `Cmd+L` (macOS) to jump to the address bar and read the URL for exact location context
- When disoriented, press `Home` to scroll to the top of the page where the repository name and tabs are always visible

</details>

<details>
<summary>Sighted users</summary>

- The H1 heading is visually the largest text near the top of the page, just below the repository tabs
- Landmarks correspond to visual regions you can already see: nav bar at top, tabs below it, main content area, and comment box at bottom
- The Elements List (NVDA+F7) is also useful for sighted users to get a structured outline of any complex page quickly

</details>

## 7. Landmark Structure by Page Type

Each GitHub page type has a consistent landmark pattern. Knowing the pattern means you can skip steps 2 and 3 above for familiar pages.

> **Landmark navigation quick reference:**
>
> - **NVDA / JAWS:** Press `D` to cycle through landmarks, `Shift+D` to go backwards
> - **VoiceOver (macOS):** Press `VO+U`, then Left/Right to select "Landmarks", then Up/Down to navigate

### Repository home page landmarks (in order)

| Landmark (what you hear with `D`) | Contains |
| ---  | ---  |
| Navigation Menu | Global nav bar - logo, search, PRs, Issues, notifications, avatar |
| Repository navigation | Code, Issues, PRs, Actions, etc. tabs |
| Main | Everything below the tabs - file tree, README |
| Repository files navigation | The rendered README specifically |

### Issues list page landmarks

| Landmark | Contains |
| ---  | ---  |
| Navigation Menu | Global nav |
| Repository navigation | Repo tabs |
| Main | Filter bar + issue list |
| Search Results List | The actual list of issues |
| Pagination | Next/previous page buttons |

### Issue detail page landmarks

| Landmark | Contains |
| ---  | ---  |
| Navigation Menu | Global nav |
| Repository navigation | Repo tabs |
| Main | Issue title, description, comments, sidebar |
| Add a comment | The reply text area and Submit button |

### Pull request Conversation tab landmarks

| Landmark | Contains |
| ---  | ---  |
| Navigation Menu | Global nav |
| Repository navigation | Repo tabs |
| Pull request tabs | Conversation, Commits, Files changed tab links |
| Main | PR description, review threads, merge section |
| Add a comment | The reply box |

### Pull request Files Changed tab landmarks

| Landmark | Contains |
| ---  | ---  |
| Navigation Menu | Global nav |
| Pull request tabs | Tab links |
| Main | File tree + diff view |
| (no "Add a comment" - inline commenting works differently) | - |

## 8. GitHub's Heading Hierarchy in Practice

GitHub uses a predictable heading structure. Learning this pattern means you can navigate any page by heading level alone.

### Repository home

```text
H1: owner/repo-name
  H2: About (sidebar section)
  H2: Releases
  H2: (README sections - whatever the author wrote)
```

### Issues list

```text
H1: Issues
  (no H2s - issues are listed as links, not headings)
  (use I for list items, or 3 for issue headings in some views)
```

### Issue detail

```text
H1: Issue title
  H2: Description
  H2: Activity
    H3: Each comment header (author + timestamp)
```

### Pull request detail - Conversation tab

```text
H1: PR title
  H2: (description, if any)
  H2: Activity
    H3: Each comment header
    H3: Each review submission
    H4: Each inline comment within a review
```

### Pull request detail - Files Changed tab

```text
H1: PR title
  H2: File tree (with "New Files Changed Experience" enabled)
    H3: Each file name heading
      H4: Each diff hunk heading
```

> **Why this matters:** Pressing `3` on a PR Files Changed tab jumps between file headings - this is how you quickly navigate to a specific file without tabbing through the entire diff.

### Learning Cards: GitHub's Heading Hierarchy

<details>
<summary>Screen reader users</summary>

- Press `1` for H1 (page identity), `2` for H2 (major sections), `3` for H3 (individual items like comments, files, or issues)
- On the PR Files Changed tab, `3` jumps between file headings and `4` jumps between diff hunks within each file
- Open the heading list (`NVDA+F7` or `Insert+F3`) and use it as a table of contents to jump directly to any section

</details>

<details>
<summary>Low vision users</summary>

- H1 headings on GitHub are displayed in large bold text near the top center of the page; H2 headings use slightly smaller bold text with a horizontal rule above them
- Issue comments (H3) each have a header bar with the author's avatar, name, and timestamp; zoom in on this bar to orient yourself in long discussions
- On the Files Changed tab, each file heading (H3) shows the file path in monospace text with a green/red summary of lines added/removed

</details>

<details>
<summary>Sighted users</summary>

- GitHub's heading hierarchy maps to visual size: H1 is the page title, H2 are section dividers, H3 are individual items within sections
- In the Issues list, issue titles function as H3 headings; scan visually or use `3` to jump between them
- On PR conversations, review comments appear in indented boxes; each box header corresponds to an H3 or H4 heading

</details>

## 9. How GitHub's Layout Changes by Viewport

GitHub is a responsive web application. The layout shifts at different screen widths, and this affects what landmarks and headings you encounter.

### At full desktop width (1200px+)

- File tree and sidebar are visible alongside the main content
- The full repository tab bar is visible
- All landmark regions described above are present

### At tablet width (768-1199px)

- Sidebar may collapse or move below the main content
- Some navigation items may move into a "More" dropdown
- Landmark structure remains the same - only visual position changes

### At mobile width (below 768px)

- Global navigation collapses to a hamburger-style menu
- Tabs may scroll horizontally or collapse
- The landmark structure is the same but the "Navigation Menu" landmark becomes a toggle

**Consistent experience recommendation:** Use your browser maximized or at full desktop width during this workshop. GitHub's landmark and heading structure is most consistent at desktop width. If you hear different landmarks or headings than described in this guide, maximize your browser window.

## 10. The Mental Model - Building Your Internal Map

After your first day of using GitHub, you will have an internal map. Here is what that map should look like:

```text
GitHub as a building:

LOBBY (global nav bar)
  Always here, same on every floor
  Contains: search, your inbox, your identity
  Landmark: "Navigation Menu"

FLOOR SELECTOR (repository nav tabs)
  Changes based on which repo you're in
  Contains: Code, Issues, PRs, Actions, Settings
  Landmark: "Repository navigation"

MAIN ROOM (the primary content area)
  Changes completely depending on which floor you're on
  Landmark: "Main"

MAILBOX (Add a comment)
  At the bottom of Issues and PR Conversation pages
  Landmark: "Add a comment"

ELEVATOR BUTTONS (keyboard shortcuts)
  G+I = Issues floor
  G+P = Pull requests floor
  G+C = Code floor
  G+A = Actions floor
  ? = Show all buttons in this building
```

When you get disoriented:

1. Press `1` - hear the H1 - know what floor you are on
2. Press `D` - hear the landmarks - know what rooms are available
3. Press `NVDA+F7` - see the full outline - know what's in the room

You are never lost. You always have these three fallbacks.

### Learning Cards: Building Your Internal Map

<details>
<summary>Screen reader users</summary>

- Memorize the elevator shortcuts: `G I` (Issues), `G P` (Pull Requests), `G C` (Code), `G A` (Actions); press `?` on any page to see the full list
- The "Add a comment" landmark is always at the bottom of Issue and PR Conversation pages; press `D` repeatedly until you hear it to jump directly to the reply box
- If a page feels unfamiliar, fall back to the three-step sequence: `1`, `D`, `NVDA+F7` and you will re-orient within seconds

</details>

<details>
<summary>Low vision users</summary>

- Think of GitHub like a building: the top bar (lobby) never changes, the tabs below it (floor selector) change per repo, and the main area (room) changes per page
- When disoriented at high zoom, press `Home` to return to the top of the page where the navigation bar and repo tabs are always visible
- The comment box ("mailbox") at the bottom of issue and PR pages has a distinct white input area with a green "Comment" button on its right

</details>

<details>
<summary>Sighted users</summary>

- The mental map is: top bar (always there), repo tabs (one row below), then main content; every GitHub page follows this three-layer stack
- Press `?` on any page to see a popup listing all keyboard shortcuts available on that specific page
- The comment box at the bottom of issues and PRs has a tabbed interface (Write/Preview) and a green Submit button; it is always the last section on the page

</details>

## Try It: The 60-Second Orientation

**Time:** 1 minute | **What you need:** A browser with your screen reader running

Open any GitHub repository - try [github.com/community-access/accessibility-agents](https://github.com/community-access/accessibility-agents) - and prove to yourself that the mental model works:

1. Press `1` - your screen reader announces the repo name. You know where you are.
2. Press `D` - you hear the first landmark. Press `D` again to hear the next one. You now know the rooms on this floor.
3. Press `2` - you jump to the first section heading. Press `2` again to scan the page structure.
4. Press `H` three times - you're moving through headings at any level. You're reading the outline.

**You're done.** Four keys, under a minute. You just navigated a GitHub repository by ear.

> **What success feels like:** You heard a repo name, at least two landmarks, and several headings. If you did, you can orient yourself on *any* GitHub page using these same four keys.

## If You Get Stuck

| Problem | What to do |
|---|---|
| Screen reader says nothing when pressing `1` | Ensure browse mode is active (NVDA: press `Escape`; JAWS: press `Num Pad Plus`). GitHub pages must fully load before heading navigation works. |
| Landmarks announce differently than expected | GitHub updates its landmark structure periodically. Press `D` to cycle landmarks and listen to what is announced rather than expecting exact names. |
| Page seems empty or broken | Some GitHub features require JavaScript. Ensure your browser has JavaScript enabled and try refreshing with `Ctrl+Shift+R`. |
| Cannot find the repository navigation tabs | Press `D` until you hear "Repository navigation" then press `K` or `Tab` to find Code, Issues, Pull Requests tabs. |
| Everything else | Post a comment on your challenge issue describing what you see and hear. A facilitator or buddy can walk you through it. |
| I finished but I am not sure I did it right | Compare your work against the [Challenge 1 reference solution](solutions/solution-01-scavenger-hunt.md). Your version does not need to match exactly -- if you explored the tabs and found the key files, you succeeded. |

## Day 2 Amplifier

> Once you have this mental model solid, the Accessibility Agents make more sense. The `@daily-briefing` agent reads your GitHub notifications and presents a structured report - but the report structure mirrors the landmark structure of GitHub itself: global activity, then per-repo activity, then per-issue and per-PR detail. The agent describes the same building you have already walked through manually.
